title: Sharp multi-instrument exclusion sensitivity and joint incompatibility tests
scope: Vector-instrument extension of the source's homogeneous linear direct-history sensitivity model, with coordinatewise supplied direct-channel bounds.
significance: Derives the exact coefficient set through a zonotope feasibility condition, including singular covariance and a concrete joint model rejection invisible in separate instrument analyses.
body:
# Sharp multi-instrument exclusion sensitivity

The manuscript's scalar-instrument sensitivity interval extends to multiple historical instruments, but the result is generally an intersection or a convex feasibility problem rather than an average of individual ratios. Instruments can jointly refute a declared direct-channel bound even when each instrument separately admits coefficients.

Let \(Z\in\mathbb R^k\) be centered with finite second moments, and let centered scalar \(D,Y\) satisfy
\[
Y=\beta D+\gamma^\top Z+u,\qquad E[Zu]=0,\qquad
|\gamma_j|\le\Gamma_j.
\tag{A}
\]
The nonnegative bounds \(\Gamma_j\) are prespecified in the chosen instrument coordinates. Define
\[
a=E[ZD],\quad b=E[ZY],\quad \Sigma=E[ZZ^\top],\quad
\mathcal Z=\{\Sigma\gamma:|\gamma_j|\le\Gamma_j\}.
\]
The exact sharp coefficient set is
\[
\mathcal B=\{\beta\in\mathbb R:b-\beta a\in\mathcal Z\}.
\tag{B}
\]
It is a convex closed subset of the real line: an interval, a point, the whole line, or empty, allowing unbounded intervals in principle.

Necessity follows by taking the vector moment of (A). For sufficiency, whenever a pair \((\beta,\gamma)\) satisfies that moment, define \(u=Y-\beta D-\gamma^\top Z\) on the observed probability space. Then \(E[Zu]=0\), and no further restrictions on the disturbance were imposed. Thus every included coefficient reproduces the full observed distribution under the declared moment model. This is the same sharpness logic as the source, now retaining all instruments simultaneously.

When \(\Sigma\) is nonsingular, write \(r=\Sigma^{-1}b\) and \(s=\Sigma^{-1}a\). The test is especially explicit:
\[
|r_j-\beta s_j|\le\Gamma_j\quad\text{for every }j.
\tag{C}
\]
For \(s_j\ne0\), this gives the interval centered at \(r_j/s_j\) with radius \(\Gamma_j/|s_j|\). Intersect all these intervals. For \(s_j=0\), that coordinate either imposes no coefficient restriction if \(|r_j|\le\Gamma_j\), or rejects the model if \(|r_j|>\Gamma_j\). No division by a zero first-stage component is needed.

For singular \(\Sigma\), (B) remains valid without a generalized-inverse shortcut that might lose a nullspace constraint. An equivalent exact characterization is
\[
|v^\top(b-\beta a)|
\le\sum_j\Gamma_j|(\Sigma v)_j|
\quad\text{for every }v\in\mathbb R^k.
\tag{D}
\]
Indeed the right side is the support function of the centrally symmetric compact convex set \(\mathcal Z\). Membership implies every inequality. Conversely, a point outside that set has a separating hyperplane and violates one such inequality. In computation, (B) is simply linear feasibility in \(\beta,\gamma\), and its endpoints can be obtained by linear optimization when bounded.

For an exact incompatibility example, take \(\Sigma=I_2\), \(a=(1,1)\), \(b=(1/2,4/5)\), and \(\Gamma_1=\Gamma_2=1/10\). Equation (C) gives \(\beta\in[2/5,3/5]\) from the first instrument and \(\beta\in[7/10,9/10]\) from the second. Each separate model is nonempty, but the joint set is empty. These moments are realizable: independent mean-zero variance-one instruments, \(D=Z_1+Z_2\), and \(Y=Z_1/2+4Z_2/5\) produce them exactly.

The rectangular bounds are coordinate-specific substantive restrictions. An invertible redefinition of instruments preserves the moment equations, but must transform the allowed direct-channel set as well; imposing the same numerical rectangle after rotation changes the model.

This result addresses exclusion sensitivity in the source population model. It does not supply weak-instrument sampling coverage for the vector problem, validate historical exclusion, or transport a local coefficient to a feasible national reform. The manuscript's separate Lipschitz transport bounds retain their own assumptions.

title: Joint reserve and maturity choice reveals a cheapest-insurance frontier
scope: Joint reserve and maturity optimization in the source's quadratic liquidity benchmark after adding an explicit positive reserve carrying cost.
significance: Solves the two-instrument problem exactly, characterizes all ties and corners, and identifies how the source's fixed-reserve comparative static changes when reserve finance is optimized.
body:
# Joint reserves and maturity: the cheapest-insurance frontier

The manuscript explicitly notes that joint reserve optimization requires a carrying cost. Adding a linear real carrying cost yields a complete two-instrument solution. It exposes a sharp substitution frontier: with identical liquidity effects, the cheaper instrument supplies all insurance unless their marginal costs coincide.

Keep the source's proceeds requirement \(B>0\), event probability \(p>0\), disruption coefficient \(c>0\), and long-maturity premium \(\tau>0\). Let \(u=mB\in[0,B]\) be long-maturity proceeds. Choose reserves \(R\ge0\) at positive carrying cost \(\zeta R\), \(\zeta>0\), measured in the same numeraire as the source objective. The joint cost is
\[
J(u,R)=\tau u+\zeta R+\frac{pc}{2}[B-u-R]_+^2.
\tag{A}
\]
The carrying cost is stipulated as a real net financing cost, not the reserve principal counted as a loss. If reserve financing has another liquidity effect, equation (A) must be changed.

No optimum has \(u+R>B\): reduce a positive instrument until total coverage equals \(B\), preserving zero disruption while strictly lowering cost. Thus put \(y=u+R\in[0,B]\). At a fixed \(y\), the least linear cost is \(hy\), where \(h=\min(\tau,\zeta)\). If \(\tau<\zeta\), the unique minimizing split is \((u,R)=(y,0)\); if \(\zeta<\tau\), it is \((0,y)\); if they are equal, every nonnegative split with sum \(y\) minimizes cost. The bound \(u\le B\) never obstructs these splits.

The remaining scalar objective is
\[
hy+\frac{pc}{2}(B-y)^2,\qquad 0\le y\le B.
\]
It is strictly convex and has unique total coverage
\[
y^*=\left[B-\frac{h}{pc}\right]_+.
\tag{B}
\]
Since \(h>0\), coverage is strictly below \(B\). All joint optima are exactly the cheapest splits of (B). In particular all-short borrowing with zero reserves is uniquely optimal when \(h\ge pcB\). When costs tie below that threshold, there is a whole line segment of equally good maturity-reserve combinations, even though total uncovered exposure is unique.

The minimum cost is
\[
J^*=
\begin{cases}
pcB^2/2,&h\ge pcB,\\
hB-h^2/(2pc),&0<h<pcB.
\end{cases}
\tag{C}
\]
The formulas agree at the threshold, and their first derivatives in \(h\) agree there as well. Below the threshold the derivative is \(B-h/(pc)=y^*\), as the envelope theorem predicts.

For a concrete comparison using the source's illustrative \(B=100\), \(p=0.1\), \(c=0.01\), \(\tau=0.02\), take reserve carrying cost \(\zeta=0.01\). Then \(h=0.01\), total coverage is ninety, and the unique optimum is all-short funding with reserves \(R=90\). Carrying cost is \(0.9\), expected disruption loss is \(0.05\), and total cost is \(0.95\). If instead \(\zeta=0.03\), long maturity is cheaper: \(u=80\), reserves zero, and total cost is \(1.8\). These are deductions from supplied hypothetical costs, not estimates of reserve policy.

The source's fixed-reserve rule shows reserves displacing long funding unit for unit locally. Joint choice adds a selection margin: changes in relative marginal costs can replace one instrument entirely by the other. Smooth coexistence would require additional curvature or distinct insurance effects.

This extension retains exogenous liquidity risk and premium, and rules out default exactly as the initial benchmark does. It does not solve the endogenous bond-pricing multiplicity shown later in the manuscript. Reserve safety, sterilization, fiscal feasibility and confidence effects must be modeled before using the frontier empirically.

title: Exact temporal allocation of least-cost permanent repair
scope: Closed-form refinement of the source's signed-control repair problem when per-date quadratic cost matrices are scalar multiples of a common positive definite matrix.
significance: Separates instrument choice from timing, derives harmonic-cost aggregation and identifies the vanishing-cost long-horizon boundary of purely quadratic repair.
body:
# Exact temporal allocation of permanent repair

The source's least-cost repair theorem handles arbitrary positive definite stacked costs. A useful specialization separates which instruments repair the permanent state from when they should be used. It also reveals a boundary of the financing model: with only quadratic costs, spreading repair over an unrestricted horizon can drive its infimum to zero.

Let \(C_0=PG\), \(b=-Pv\), and suppose \(b\in{\rm range}(C_0)\), as required for feasibility. Retain signed instruments and a finite horizon \(T\ge1\). Specialize the cost to
\[
J(U)=\frac12\sum_{s=0}^{T-1}w_su_s^\top R_0u_s,\qquad
w_s>0,\quad R_0\succ0,
\]
with repair constraint \(C_0\sum_su_s=b\). Put
\[
H_T=\sum_{s=0}^{T-1}w_s^{-1},\qquad
M=C_0R_0^{-1}C_0^\top.
\]

For any fixed aggregate instrument vector \(a=\sum_su_s\), the unique least-cost timing is
\[
u_s=\frac{a}{w_sH_T},
\qquad
J_{\min}(a)=\frac{a^\top R_0a}{2H_T}.
\tag{A}
\]
One can prove this without matrix differentiation. Set \(e_s=u_s-a/(w_sH_T)\), so \(\sum_se_s=0\). Expanding the cost yields
\[
\sum_sw_su_s^\top R_0u_s
=\frac{a^\top R_0a}{H_T}
+\sum_sw_se_s^\top R_0e_s.
\]
The cross terms cancel because their sum is proportional to \(\sum_se_s\). Positive definiteness makes the remainder nonnegative, with equality only when every \(e_s=0\). This proves both optimality and uniqueness.

It remains to choose the aggregate \(a\) subject to \(C_0a=b\). The source's single-period quadratic argument gives
\[
a^*=R_0^{-1}C_0^\top M^+b.
\]
Combining with (A), the full unique solution and cost are
\[
u_s^*=\frac{R_0^{-1}C_0^\top M^+b}{w_sH_T},
\qquad
J_T^*=\frac{b^\top M^+b}{2H_T}.
\tag{B}
\]
The pseudoinverse is required if some permanent-state coordinates are redundant. Feasibility still means \(b\) belongs to the range; (B) does not repair an unreachable displacement. If \(b=0\), the unique minimum is zero controls.

With equal date costs \(w_s=1\), each date uses \(a^*/T\), and cost is the one-date minimum divided by \(T\). Thus, whenever nonzero repair is feasible, \(J_T^*>0\) for each finite horizon but \(J_T^*\to0\) as \(T\to\infty\). This is an infimum across different finite-horizon problems. No finite sequence attains zero cost for nonzero \(b\), because positive definite costs make zero cost require every control to vanish.

If date-zero costs are discounted at factor \(\delta\in(0,1)\), so \(w_s=\delta^s\), the optimal timing weights are proportional to \(\delta^{-s}\): later instruments are cheaper in the stated accounting. The same aggregate permanent repair is achieved, but this least-cost criterion favors postponement. That observation is conditional on disregarding the welfare cost of living with the damage while repair is delayed.

This matters for interpreting the source's distinction between permanent repair and discounted welfare. Permanent-state effects depend only on the sum of controls, whereas its equation (4) values their timing and transitory responses. Adding linear resource costs, deadlines, intensity caps, discount-weighted capacity benefits or irreversible exit can prevent the vanishing-cost comparison. None can be inferred from the quadratic minimum alone.

The result is an exact timing refinement within the finite-dimensional invariant accumulation model. It does not identify the permanent projection, establish that observed recessions have permanent effects, or extend signed-control feasibility to nonnegative instruments. No empirical or external-literature claim is used.
